order.why_here: The template for the chapter: a dict of what you have seen, queried with a complement, check before insert.
Same one-pass dict, but the value stored is the last index, and overwriting keeps it the nearest.
Shows the memory can shrink to a candidate and a counter when the question only needs a summary.
The smallest possible memory: one running count that a zero resets, the seed of every running accumulator.
Back to sets, now 27 of them at once, with arithmetic that routes each cell to its sets.
The dict key stops being the item itself: design a canonical key so equal keys mean the same group.
Count with a dict, then use the counts themselves as array indices: bucket sort instead of comparison sort.
Introduces prefix and suffix accumulation: 'all but one' becomes 'left part times right part'.
A set plus a start-of-run test, and the chapter's first real amortised argument for a nested loop.
Prefix sums meet the two sum dict: count earlier prefixes equal to the current prefix minus k.
Designing an unambiguous representation: length-prefixed serialisation that no content can confuse.
The array becomes its own hash table, parking value v at index v - 1, for O(1) extra space.
Pigeonhole buckets on the number line replace sorting; the answer must cross a bucket boundary.
Value buckets of width t + 1 combined with a sliding window of indices from contains duplicate II.
Counting pairs across positions: merge sort counts how many smaller elements jump from the right half.
The same merge-sort count, but the counted condition differs from the merge order, so counting gets its own pass.
Counting by value with a Fenwick tree, the general tool behind the previous two problems.
